lessons.title: The Protective Put: Setting a Floor Under a Stock You Own

children.text: On 11 March 2025, IndusInd Bank shares fell about 27% in a single session after the bank disclosed discrepancies in its derivatives accounting. The Nifty 50 barely moved that day. If IndusInd was one of twenty stocks in a mutual fund, it was a bad day. If it was a large chunk of your personal wealth, it was a disaster that no index hedge could have softened. Single-stock risk needs a single-stock answer, and the classic one is the protective put. This lesson turns the idea from Chapter 1 into a complete tool: what the floor is, what it costs, where breakeven sits, and when it is worth using.

body.text: A protective put turns an open-ended downside into a known floor. Your worst-case selling price is the strike minus the premium, fixed on the day you buy the put, however bad the news gets.

stats.label: IndusInd Bank, 11 March 2025
stats.context: In one session, after an accounting disclosure

stats.label: Nifty 50, same day
stats.context: An index put would have paid nothing

stats.label: Adani Enterprises, early 2023
stats.context: Within about two weeks of the Hindenburg report

markDefs.definition: Holding shares and buying a put option on the same shares, so that the put's gains offset the shares' losses below the strike.

children.text: is two positions held together: the shares you already own and a put on those same shares. Above the strike, the put is worthless and you simply own the stock. Below the strike, every rupee the stock loses is matched by a rupee the put gains. The loss stops at the strike, and the premium is the price of that stop. Three numbers define the whole position.

body.latex: \begin{aligned} \text{Floor price} &= K - P \\ \text{Maximum loss per share} &= (S_0 - K) + P \\ \text{Breakeven} &= S_0 + P \end{aligned}
body.caption: S₀ = price when the put is bought (or your reference price), K = strike, P = premium per share

children.text: Worked Example: A Floor Under a Bank Stock

Suppose Pooja, a 45-year-old architect in Hyderabad, held 1,000 IndusInd Bank shares at about ₹900 in early March 2025, worth ₹9,00,000 and nearly a third of her equity savings. Assume one option lot is 500 shares, so two lots cover her holding. She buys two lots of the one-month 850 put at ₹12.

stats.label: Floor price
stats.context: 850 − 12. Her holding cannot be worth less than ₹8,38,000 at expiry

stats.label: Breakeven
stats.context: 900 + 12. The stock must rise ₹12 to cover the cost of cover

body.caption: Pooja's 1,000 shares at expiry, with and without the 850 put bought at ₹12 (illustrative premium)

body.title: Profit or loss at expiry: shares alone vs shares with a protective put

children.text: The chart shows the whole story. Unprotected, the line keeps falling with the stock. Protected, it goes flat at −₹62,000 below the strike and runs parallel to the unprotected line above it, just ₹12,000 lower. On a ₹656 close, the difference between the two is ₹1,82,000. On a quiet month, the protection costs her ₹12,000.

body.title: Find the breakeven
body.question: Pooja bought the protective put when the stock was at ₹900, using the 850 put at ₹12. At what stock price at expiry does her combined position exactly break even?
body.explanation: Breakeven = S₀ + P = 900 + 12 = ₹912. At ₹912 the shares gain ₹12 each, exactly paying for the ₹12 premium. ₹838 is the floor price, which is a different number: it is the lowest effective value of her shares.

children.text: Choosing the Strike on a Single Stock
The deductible logic from Lesson 4 of Chapter 1 applies directly. Individual stocks are more volatile than the Nifty, so the same distance from the current price costs more. Here are Pooja's choices.

body.caption: One-month puts on a ₹900 stock, 1,000 shares (illustrative premiums)

body.text: Compare this with the Nifty table in Chapter 1. A three-month Nifty put 4% below cost about 1% of the portfolio. Here, a one-month put 6% below a single stock costs about 1.3%. Single-stock protection is expensive because single stocks are volatile, and that cost repeats every month you want to stay covered. This is why protective puts on individual stocks are best used for specific, time-bound risks, not held forever.

body.title: Calculate the floor
body.prompt: Rahul holds 300 L&T shares at an illustrative ₹3,600. He buys a put with a strike of ₹3,400 at a premium of ₹55. What is his floor price per share, in rupees?
body.explanation: Floor price = K − P = 3,400 − 55 = ₹3,345. His maximum loss per share is (3,600 − 3,400) + 55 = ₹255, about 7.1% of ₹3,600, and his breakeven is 3,600 + 55 = ₹3,655.

body.title: Breakeven rule
body.textWithBlank: The breakeven of a protective put is the share price when the put was bought ___ the premium paid.
body.explanation: The premium is a sunk cost, so the shares must rise by the premium amount before the combined position shows a profit.

children.text: When a Protective Put Makes Sense, and When It Does Not

body.title: Good and poor uses of a single-stock protective put

columns.label: Good fit
points: A concentrated holding you cannot or will not sell right now
A known event ahead: quarterly results, a court verdict, a regulatory decision
Large unrealised gains you want to protect while delaying a sale
Holding size at or above one full lot
Stock with liquid options and tight bid-ask spreads

columns.label: Poor fit
points: A stock that is a small slice of a diversified portfolio
Permanent protection rolled month after month
Holding smaller than one lot, forcing you to over-hedge
Stock not in the F&O segment, or with thinly traded options
Replacing a decision you should make: whether to own the stock at all

body.text: Stock options on NSE are physically settled. If Pooja's 850 put is in the money at expiry, she is treated as selling 1,000 shares at ₹850, and those shares leave her demat account. If she wants to keep the stock after the event, she should sell the put in the market before expiry and keep the cash gain instead. Closing before expiry is also usually cheaper once transaction taxes are counted, which Chapter 5 covers.

body.title: The ESOP holder who wants a floor
body.scenario: Vivek, 39, is a senior vice president at a listed Indian IT services company in Pune and is classified as a designated person under the company's insider trading code. Over ten years he has built up ESOP shares now worth ₹1.1 crore, about 70% of his net worth. The company's options trade actively on NSE. Ahead of the next quarterly results, he plans to buy protective puts on his company's stock.
body.prompt: Can Vivek do this? If not, what are his realistic alternatives for reducing his concentration risk?
body.modelAnswer:
1. He almost certainly cannot. Under SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, company codes of conduct bar designated persons from taking positions in derivatives on their own company's shares. Buying puts on his employer's stock would breach that, regardless of his intention to hedge.
2. Alternative one: sell shares in stages during open trading windows, following pre-clearance rules, or through a pre-approved trading plan under the regulations. This removes the risk directly.
3. Alternative two: diversify the proceeds into broad index funds or other assets. Capital gains tax on the sale is a real cost, but it has to be weighed against the risk of holding 70% of his net worth in one stock.
4. Alternative three: he could hedge part of his general equity market exposure with Nifty options, as long as it complies with his company's code. But this does nothing for company-specific risk like a bad quarter or a governance issue.
5. He should check his company's code of conduct and speak to the compliance officer before any transaction.
The lesson: the protective put is a great tool, but it is not available to everyone for every stock. For corporate insiders, reducing concentration is usually the only real hedge.

body.title: What if my holding is smaller than one lot, or my stock has no options?

children.text: Only stocks in NSE's F&O segment have options, a list of a little over 200 names that changes periodically, and option lots can be worth several lakh rupees. Two common situations follow:

if you own 300 shares and the lot is 500, one put covers 200 shares you do not own. Those extra 200 puts are a bet on the stock falling. Either accept the partial over-hedge knowingly, or use a different tool.
you can only hedge the market part of its risk with index options, which leaves company-specific risk untouched. Trimming the position or setting a clear exit rule is often the more honest answer.

A stop-loss order is sometimes suggested as a free alternative. It is not the same thing. A stop-loss sells you out after the fall and cannot protect you when a stock opens far below your stop, as IndusInd did. A put fixes your selling price in advance, gap or no gap.

body.label: Protective put vs stop-loss
body.value: A put guarantees the price. A stop-loss only triggers an order.
body.context: On a gap-down open, a stop-loss can fill far below its trigger. A put's strike holds regardless of how the stock opens.

body.title: Before you buy a protective put on a stock
steps: Confirm the stock is in NSE's F&O segment and note the current lot size.
Check that your holding is at least one full lot, and decide how many lots match it without over-hedging.
Name the specific risk and date you are protecting against, and pick an expiry that covers it.
Calculate the floor price, maximum loss and breakeven for two or three strikes.
Check the bid-ask spread on your chosen strike, and if you are a designated person at a listed company, check your insider trading code before doing anything.

body.label: NSE: Underlyings in the F&O Segment
body.description: The current list of stocks and indices with derivatives on NSE, with their lot sizes.

cards.definition: Owning shares and buying a put on the same shares to cap the loss below the strike.
Strike minus premium. The lowest effective value of each protected share at expiry.
Price when bought + premium. The stock must rise this far to cover the cost of cover.
The risk that a stock opens far below its previous close, skipping past stop-loss levels. A put protects against it, a stop-loss does not.
An employee covered by a listed company's insider trading code, typically barred from derivatives on the company's own shares.

points: A protective put is shares plus a put on those shares. Below the strike, the put's gains offset the stock's losses.
Floor price = K − P, maximum loss = (S₀ − K) + P, breakeven = S₀ + P.
Single-stock protection costs more than index protection because individual stocks are more volatile.
It works best for concentrated holdings facing a specific, time-bound risk, with a holding of at least one lot.
Stock options are physically settled, so sell the put before expiry if you want to keep your shares.
A stop-loss is not a substitute: it cannot protect against a gap-down open. Corporate insiders usually cannot use stock puts at all.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Price moves for IndusInd Bank and Adani Enterprises are approximate. The investor examples, lot sizes and option premiums are illustrative. Insider trading rules vary by company code, so employees of listed companies must consult their compliance officer. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before using options.
